case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel River Expeditions (KRE) is a partnership in the adventure tourism and outdoor leisure sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2013 by Sofia Almeida and two partners, it runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and sells 14,000 units a year, one unit being a paid rafting place at an average selling price of $120. KRE plans to invest $640,000 in new rafts and a riverside activity centre, financed by a $240,000 hire-purchase agreement and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a variable cost of $40 a unit. A recent gear inspection found a 4.2% defect rate in safety equipment and guide absence has reached 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Safety and Operations Log, Q3 2025: KRE ran 3,500 expedition places with 12 incident reports, down from 19 last season, and a 4.2% defect rate in inspected buoyancy aids and helmets. Guide absence affected 8% of scheduled trips. Feedback from 640 participants showed 72% rated safety briefings as clear and 66% would pay $9 more for upgraded wetsuit hire. Of 70 staff, 26 guides have not completed on-the-job safety refresher training; off-the-job swiftwater-rescue courses cost $620 per guide.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel River Expeditions as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Outdoor-Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.50% to 4.25%, increasing the cost of KRE's $240,000 hire-purchase finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.53 to $14.35 an hour from April 2026, affecting seasonal guide pay. (3) Diesel and equipment input costs have risen 13.4%, adventure-tourism demand grew 5.8% and consumer inflation is running at 5.5%.

questions.question_text: KRE plans to fund part of its new rafts and activity centre with a $240,000 hire-purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for KRE of using the $400,000 retained profit instead of more hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $400,000 retained profit avoids the interest charges and fixed periodic instalments attached to the $240,000 hire-purchase agreement, which matters for a seasonal rafting business whose cash inflows are concentrated in summer. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year already committed and the base rate rising to 4.25%, every dollar of retained profit spent now is a dollar of finance cost avoided, protecting the $80 contribution earned on each of the 14,000 expedition places.

Point 2: Retained profit gives KRE immediate ownership of the new rafts and centre without a hire-purchase lender holding title until the final payment, so the partnership is not exposed to repossession if a poor season reduces bookings. It also preserves the partners' control: no finance company can impose conditions on how Sofia Almeida and her partners run the riverside operation. Drawing on the $400,000 first reduces the hire-purchase balance actually required, cutting KRE's fixed commitments while it deals with a 4.2% defect rate in safety gear and 8% guide absence.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KRE's seasonal cash flow and expansion funding.

questions.question_text: KRE is launching its new riverside activity centre. Consider local radio advertising, leaflets in tourist offices, and social media adventure influencers. Which should KRE choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Regional radio can reach holidaymakers already in the area and announce the new centre quickly at modest cost, with flexible messages about availability. Its limitation is that audio cannot show the rapids or the riverside setting, and the audience includes many people who will never book a rafting trip, so a share of the spend is wasted while KRE is funding a $640,000 investment.

Leaflets in tourist offices: Printed leaflets placed in regional visitor centres target people actively planning outdoor activities and are cheap to produce, with a tangible design that can show the centre. They suffer from very narrow reach and no measurable response; most tourists never visit a tourist office, so leaflets alone cannot sell the 14,000 expedition places needed to justify the new rafts and centre.

Social media adventure influencers: Outdoor and travel influencers can show the rafting experience on video to precisely the audience identified in KRE's feedback — the 72% of 640 participants who value clear safety briefings and the 66% who would pay $9 more for upgraded wetsuit hire. Content is shareable and results are measurable, though it takes time to build and depends on choosing influencers with genuine credibility in adventure tourism.

Recommendation: KRE should choose social media adventure influencers as the main channel, supported by low-cost leaflets in tourist offices. Influencers demonstrate the experience visually and reach the safety-conscious, experience-seeking segment that underpins the $640,000 centre, at a cost controllable from the $400,000 retained profit. Local radio is rejected because it cannot display the activity and reaches too many non-customers; leaflets alone are rejected because their reach is too narrow to fill 14,000 places. Influencer content can be reused across channels, giving better value while the partnership services $240,000 of hire-purchase finance.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to KRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KRE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KRE with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and leaflets are rejected.

questions.question_text: KRE has a 4.2% defect rate in safety equipment and 8% guide absence. Explain two benefits for KRE of its autocratic leadership style in addressing these issues.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Sofia Almeida set clear, non-negotiable safety rules and enforce equipment checks without delay, which directly targets the 4.2% defect rate in buoyancy aids and helmets. In a safety-critical adventure business, one decision-maker can withdraw faulty gear and stop a trip immediately, protecting the 72% of participants who rate briefings as clear and reducing the 12 incident reports. Quick, uniform decisions are more reliable than waiting for consensus when safety is at stake.

Point 2: A clear chain of command also helps manage the 8% guide absence: the leader can reallocate guides and cancel or merge trips decisively, keeping the 14,000 expedition-place target on track and avoiding the capacity loss that would erode the $80 contribution per place. Consistent instructions from the top ensure that every guide follows the same safety procedure, which supports the plan to invest $640,000 in new rafts and the riverside centre. Autocratic leadership therefore gives KRE the rapid, standardised control that its safety and absence problems demand, even if it may limit staff input.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KRE's defect rate, absence and safety.

questions.question_text: KRE must retrain 26 guides on new safety equipment. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job swiftwater-rescue courses. Which should KRE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Safety refresher training on KRE's own rafts and equipment uses the exact buoyancy aids and helmets that showed the 4.2% defect rate, so guides learn to inspect the gear they will actually use. It costs no course fees, keeps guides available for the 14,000 expedition places and can be delivered between trips, which suits a seasonal operation servicing $240,000 of hire-purchase finance. The drawback is that senior guides acting as trainers are taken off the water, and if their own inspection habits are weak the defect rate may not fall consistently.

Off-the-job training: The swiftwater-rescue course at $620 per guide gives recognised, up-to-date rescue skills for all 26 guides, costing 26 × $620 = $16,120 — a modest sum against the $640,000 investment and affordable from the $400,000 retained profit. It also brings an external standard that can reassure participants, 72% of whom value clear safety briefings. However, it removes guides from trips for several days during the season, risking cancelled expeditions and lost $120 per-place revenue, and generic course content may need adaptation to KRE's own river.

Decision: KRE should choose on-the-job training first, with off-the-job rescue courses scheduled for the closed season. On-the-job training directly addresses the 4.2% defect rate on the actual equipment, costs less and avoids losing guides during the operating season when 8% absence already strains cover. Full off-the-job training now is rejected because the short-term loss of 26 guides would cut capacity and revenue while the new rafts are being introduced; the $16,120 course can be added later without that disruption.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of KRE.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, seasonal disruption and safety relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KRE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($120 − $40) = $280,000 ÷ $80 = 3,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,500 expedition places a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $120 − $40 = $80. Answer: contribution per unit is $80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KRE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 3,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 14,000 expedition places: KRE has a margin of safety of 14,000 − 3,500 = 10,500 units, showing how much demand can fall before the $280,000 fixed costs are uncovered, useful given 8% guide absence.
2. Use contribution per unit of $80 to test the $9 wetsuit-hire premium: adding $9 would raise contribution to $89, indicating the extra revenue available to service the $240,000 hire-purchase agreement.
3. Set volume targets for the $640,000 centre: 8,000 extra expedition places at $80 contribution generate $640,000, so managers can track how quickly the investment is covered.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $280,000 ÷ 14,000 + $40 = $60.00 a place and labour productivity of 14,000 ÷ 70 = 200 places per employee, giving a baseline to monitor the 13.4% diesel and equipment cost rise and the effect of guide absence.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $80 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 10,500 expedition places; $9 premium and pricing analysis; volume targets for the $640,000 centre; and unit-cost benchmarking at $60.00 with labour productivity of 200 places per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KRE's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KRE's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.45 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $100,000; 2025 current assets = $35,000 + $60,000 + $65,000 = $160,000. Coverage of short-term obligations 2024 = $100,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.00; 2025 = $160,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.45. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($100,000 − $30,000) ÷ $100,000 = $70,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.70; 2025 = ($160,000 − $35,000) ÷ $110,000 = $125,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.14.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved markedly. Coverage of short-term obligations rose from 1.00 to 1.45 as current assets increased by $60,000 while current liabilities grew only $10,000 to $110,000. The stock-excluding measure rose from 0.70 to 1.14, so KRE can now meet its short-term debts from receivables and cash alone rather than relying on selling equipment stock — important while it services $240,000 of hire-purchase finance. The improvement is driven mainly by cash rising from $25,000 to $65,000 and receivables from $45,000 to $60,000. Trade receivables are still higher, so slower-paying tour operators could weaken the position, but the larger cash balance gives a real cushion for the $640,000 centre plan.

Conclusion: KRE's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025, and the 0.70 to 1.14 move in the stock-excluding measure is the clearest evidence that underlying liquidity is stronger. KRE should keep monitoring receivables but can proceed with the activity centre from a sounder short-term position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion that liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KRE of offering the upgraded wetsuit hire that 66% of surveyed participants would pay $9 more for.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The 66% of 640 participants who would pay $9 more for upgraded wetsuit hire gives KRE a way to raise contribution per expedition place from $80 towards $89 without selling more places, directly improving coverage of the $280,000 fixed costs and the $240,000 hire-purchase commitment. Combined with the 72% who rate safety briefings as clear, a better wetsuit offering reinforces KRE's safety reputation and supports the $120 price while diesel and equipment input costs rise 13.4%.

Disadvantage: Buying upgraded wetsuits requires more capital at a time when KRE is already investing $640,000 in new rafts and the riverside centre, and the survey records willingness to pay rather than guaranteed demand, so the $9 premium may not be realised on every place. If only a minority actually pay it, the extra purchase cost would raise the $40 variable cost per unit and squeeze contribution. The 4.2% defect rate in existing safety gear also shows that managing equipment quality is already a problem; adding more kit to inspect could increase the inspection burden if guide absence stays at 8%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KRE's survey, costs and safety record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.4% rise in diesel and equipment input costs will affect KRE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.25%): If KRE's $240,000 hire-purchase cost tracks the base rate, the extra annual finance charge is 0.75% of $240,000 = $1,800 (0.0075 × $240,000). This is small beside fixed costs of $280,000 and can be limited by agreeing a fixed rate on the new rafts. The main risk is that dearer credit makes future expansion finance more costly, but the direct effect on this year's costs is minor.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.35 an hour): Guides are hourly paid, so this rise increases KRE's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual figure can be invented; the honest judgement is qualitative against the given 200 expedition places per employee and $80 contribution per place. With guide absence at 8%, any loss of productivity would compound the wage rise, but higher prices or the $9 wetsuit premium could offset part of it.

Diesel and equipment input costs (13.4%): These affect every one of the 14,000 expedition places and the running of the new rafts. The insert does not decompose the $40 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 13.4%, that adds 13.4% × $40 = $5.36 a place, or about $75,040 a year (14,000 × $5.36). Even a narrower rise would reduce the $80 contribution needed to fund the $640,000 centre. Premium pricing and fuel-efficient vehicles can recover only part of this.

Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in diesel and equipment costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 14,000 places and directly erodes the $80 contribution underpinning the $640,000 investment, whereas the interest rise is small and hedgeable and the wage rise can be absorbed through productivity and pricing. Input-cost inflation therefore demands the most urgent response from the partners.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KRE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of KRE with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
